phases.title: Phase 0 · Why Claude Code Exists
phases.description: Start from zero. Understand the problem Claude Code solves before touching commands.

modules.title: Why Claude Code exists
modules.objective: Understand why Claude Code is different from a normal chatbot or autocomplete tool.
modules.simple: A chatbot answers questions. Claude Code can also inspect a real project, edit files, run commands, test results, and continue working through a task. You still decide the goal and approve important actions.
modules.problem: A normal chat window does not automatically understand your project folder, run its tests, or change its files safely.
modules.analogy: A chatbot is like a teacher who explains from a desk. Claude Code is like a helper who can enter your workshop, inspect the tools, do a small job, and show you what changed.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code runs inside a terminal, sees the folder you opened, uses tools such as file reading and command execution, and asks for permission before sensitive actions.
whenNotToUse: Giving it uncontrolled production access
Asking it to change everything without a clear goal
Trusting results without review
modules.enableDisable: There is nothing to enable in this concept. You start Claude Code only when you want it, and exit the session when finished.
usage: Ask it to explain the folder without editing
procedure: Move to a small practice folder.
Ask: ‘Explain this folder for a beginner. Do not edit anything.’
Check whether every file it mentions exists.
failureModes: Assuming it knows files outside the current project
Approving commands you do not understand
Treating a confident answer as proof
commonMistakes: Using an important production repository on day one
Giving a vague request such as ‘make it better’
modules.bad: Improve this entire project.
modules.good: Explain the five most important files in this practice folder. Do not edit or run commands.
modules.exercise: Compare the same question in a normal chatbot and Claude Code. Write down what Claude Code can inspect that the chatbot cannot.
modules.interviewQuestion: How is an AI coding agent different from a chatbot or autocomplete assistant?
modules.advanced: Later you will learn that Claude Code is an agentic coding environment because it combines language-model reasoning with tools, project context, permissions, and feedback loops.
modules.success: You can explain why Claude Code exists and name at least three differences from a normal chatbot.
modules.summary: Claude Code is useful because it can work with a real project, not only discuss code in isolation.

quiz.question: What is the safest first use of Claude Code?
options: Explain a practice folder without editing
quiz.explanation: Explanation-only work lets you learn the tool with minimal risk.

phases.title: Phase 1 · Meet Claude Code
phases.description: Learn the terminal, folders, repositories, permissions, installation, and your first safe edit.

modules.title: Terminal, folders, files, and commands
modules.objective: Understand the basic environment Claude Code works inside.
modules.simple: The terminal is a text window where you type commands. A folder is a container for files. Claude Code works mainly with the folder you open it from.
modules.problem: Without knowing the current folder, a beginner can accidentally let Claude inspect or change the wrong project.
modules.analogy: A folder is a room. The terminal is the doorway. Claude Code can mainly see the room you brought it into.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code reads the current working directory and uses terminal tools to inspect and operate on files there.
whenToUse: When checking where a command will run
whenNotToUse: Do not start from a broad folder such as your entire home directory
Do not work in system folders while learning
modules.enableDisable: Folders and terminal commands are operating-system features. You do not enable them in Claude Code. You control scope by changing the current directory before starting Claude.
usage: Use pwd or Get-Location to see the current folder
Use ls or dir to list files
Use cd to move into a folder
procedure: Run `pwd` on macOS/Linux or `Get-Location` in PowerShell.
Create or open a safe practice folder.
failureModes: Running commands copied from the internet without understanding them
commonMistakes: Confusing a file with a folder
Assuming Claude automatically knows every project on the computer
modules.bad: Start Claude from C:\ or / and ask it to inspect everything.
modules.good: Create a folder named claude-practice, enter it, confirm the path, then start Claude there.
modules.exercise: Create a practice folder with one text file, list the folder contents, and explain what each terminal command did.
modules.interviewQuestion: Why does the current working directory matter to an AI coding assistant?
modules.advanced: Power users use worktrees, containers, and restricted mounts to create stronger project boundaries.
modules.success: You can open the terminal, navigate to a folder, list files, and confirm Claude will start in the intended location.
modules.summary: The current folder defines the first and most important safety boundary.

quiz.question: What should you check before starting Claude Code?
quiz.explanation: Claude Code works against the project context in the current folder.

modules.title: Install, start, exit, update, and uninstall Claude Code
modules.objective: Install and control Claude Code safely.
modules.simple: Installation puts the Claude command on your computer. Starting opens a session. Exiting stops the session. Updating replaces the installed version with a newer one.
modules.problem: Beginners often copy installation commands for the wrong operating system or do not know how to stop or remove the tool.
modules.analogy: Installing is bringing a tool into your workshop. Starting is switching it on. Exiting is switching it off. Uninstalling removes it.
modules.howClaudeImplements: The command-line program authenticates with your account, opens an interactive session, and communicates with Claude while using local tools under permission controls.
whenToUse: Install once on a supported machine
Update when required by official release guidance
whenNotToUse: Do not use unofficial installers
Do not paste Linux shell commands directly into Windows PowerShell unless documented
modules.enableDisable: Start with the `claude` command. Exit using the documented exit command or terminal interrupt. Disable use by closing the session; uninstall using the official installation method's removal steps.
usage: Follow official installation instructions for your OS
procedure: Verify your operating system and shell.
Use the current official installation documentation.
commonMistakes: Running shell scripts in PowerShell without a compatible shell
modules.bad: Copy the first installation command found on a random blog.
modules.good: Use official documentation, verify the shell, install, run help, and test inside a disposable folder.
modules.exercise: Install Claude Code, capture the version/help output, start it in a practice folder, and exit without making changes.
modules.interviewQuestion: What checks should an enterprise team perform before installing an AI coding CLI?
modules.advanced: Enterprise environments may manage versions, authentication, proxy certificates, settings, and allowed tools centrally.
modules.success: You can install, start, stop, update, and explain how to remove Claude Code.
modules.summary: Use the correct official installation path for your operating system and know how to stop the session before doing real work.

quiz.question: Where should a beginner get installation instructions?
quiz.explanation: Installation instructions change and must come from the official source.

modules.title: Permissions: read, edit, and run
modules.objective: Understand every permission request before approving it.
modules.simple: Reading looks at information. Editing changes files. Running executes a command. These actions have different risks.
modules.problem: Approving every permission request removes the main safety checkpoint between a request and its consequences.
modules.analogy: Reading is letting someone look at a document. Editing is letting them write on it. Running a command is letting them operate a machine.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code presents permission prompts or follows configured permission rules before tool actions.
whenToUse: Allow safe reads in the intended project
Allow specific edits after reviewing scope
whenNotToUse: Do not approve deletion, deployment, secret access, or broad shell commands you do not understand
modules.enableDisable: Permissions can be approved interactively and managed through Claude Code settings. Keep broad bypass modes disabled while learning.
usage: Check the exact path or command
Approve, deny, or ask Claude to explain
procedure: Ask Claude to read one file.
Ask it to propose an edit without applying it.
Deny an unrelated or unclear command.
commonMistakes: Using skip-permissions mode on a host machine
modules.bad: Allow every command for convenience.
modules.good: Allow exact read and test operations, review edits, and keep destructive or external actions behind approval.
modules.exercise: Create a table classifying ten example actions as read, edit, execute, external, reversible, or irreversible.
modules.interviewQuestion: How do permission boundaries reduce the blast radius of an AI agent?
modules.advanced: Architects combine permission rules with containers, read-only mounts, separate credentials, policy hooks, and human approval gates.
modules.success: You can explain what a requested action will do and deny it when its scope is unclear.
modules.summary: Permissions are not interruptions; they are control points.

quiz.question: Which action needs the most caution?
quiz.explanation: Deployment creates external and potentially irreversible consequences.

modules.title: Your first practical project
modules.objective: Complete a safe end-to-end task with Claude Code.
modules.simple: You will create a tiny web page, ask Claude to explain it, make one change, run it, inspect the result, and undo the change.
modules.problem: Theory does not teach the full loop of asking, approving, editing, checking, and recovering.
modules.analogy: Learning Claude Code is like learning to drive in an empty parking area before entering traffic.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude reads the project, proposes a change, edits the selected file, and can run a local command or check.
whenToUse: Testing a new Claude Code configuration
whenNotToUse: Do not use production code for this first exercise
modules.enableDisable: No special feature is required. Use a normal interactive session with default permissions.
procedure: Ask Claude to explain every section.
Ask it to change only the heading.
Ask Claude to show the diff.
Undo the change using Git or a backup.
commonMistakes: Building a full application as the first task
modules.bad: Build me a complete SaaS application.
modules.good: In index.html, change only the h1 text from Hello to Welcome. Show the exact diff and do not touch any other file.
modules.exercise: Complete the full explain-edit-check-undo loop twice with different text changes.
modules.interviewQuestion: What controls make an AI-assisted code change reviewable and reversible?
modules.advanced: The same loop later expands to tests, commits, pull requests, independent review, and deployment gates.
modules.success: You completed a verified change and reverted it without losing the project.
modules.summary: A safe Claude Code workflow is small, visible, testable, and reversible.

quiz.question: What should happen after Claude edits a file?
quiz.explanation: Verification confirms the edit matches the request.

phases.title: Phase 2 · Everyday Claude Code
phases.description: Learn prompts, project exploration, Git, sessions, debugging, tests, and routine feature work.

modules.title: How to talk to Claude Code
modules.objective: Write requests that produce reviewable work.
modules.simple: A useful request contains the desired result, relevant context, boundaries, and a check.
modules.problem: Vague requests force Claude to guess what success means.
modules.analogy: Telling a builder ‘make the house better’ is vague. Telling them ‘repair the leaking kitchen tap without replacing the sink’ is actionable.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude combines your request with project evidence and tool results to choose actions.
whenNotToUse: Do not overload one prompt with unrelated tasks
modules.enableDisable: Prompting is always available. You control behaviour by adding or removing constraints, examples, and approval gates.
procedure: Ask for a plan when risk is meaningful.
Ask for changed files and remaining risks.
commonMistakes: Saying cleaner, better, or production-ready without criteria
modules.bad: Make login better.
modules.good: Add a visible error message when login credentials are invalid. Keep the existing API contract. First locate the current login flow, then implement and run the relevant tests. Report changed files.
modules.exercise: Rewrite five vague software tasks into executable briefs.
modules.interviewQuestion: What information should an engineering prompt include to reduce ambiguity?
modules.advanced: At scale, prompts become reusable skills, task schemas, issue templates, and machine-readable acceptance criteria.
modules.success: Another engineer can understand the result, limits, and verification without asking basic questions.
modules.summary: Good prompts define outcomes and evidence, not just activity.

quiz.question: Which prompt element proves completion?
quiz.explanation: A check creates observable evidence.

modules.title: Understand an unfamiliar repository
modules.objective: Create a trustworthy project map before editing.
modules.simple: A repository is a project folder tracked by Git. Ask Claude to find entry points, important folders, run commands, tests, and data flow.
modules.problem: Changing code without understanding its callers and tests creates hidden breakage.
modules.analogy: Before repairing a building, inspect the blueprint, power lines, and water pipes.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude reads manifests, documentation, source files, tests, and version history to build an evidence-based map.
whenNotToUse: Do not ask it to read every file without a question
modules.enableDisable: Repository exploration uses normal read tools. Keep editing disabled by explicitly saying ‘do not edit.’
modules.bad: Read the repo and tell me everything.
modules.good: Map the login request from UI to persistence. Cite files and symbols, identify tests, and do not edit.
modules.exercise: Create a project map for a small open-source repository and manually verify every file reference.
modules.interviewQuestion: How would you use an AI coding agent to understand an unfamiliar codebase safely?
modules.advanced: Large repositories need layered maps, code ownership, dependency graphs, and scoped CLAUDE.md files.
modules.success: You can predict which files and checks a small change is likely to affect.
modules.summary: Explore by execution path and evidence, not by reading everything.

quiz.question: What should repository exploration produce?
quiz.explanation: A map connects files to behaviour and checks.

modules.title: Git, diffs, commits, and undo
modules.objective: Make every change visible and reversible.
modules.simple: Git records project history. A diff shows what changed. A commit saves a named checkpoint.
modules.problem: Without version control, AI edits can be difficult to review or undo.
modules.analogy: Git is a save-history system for a project, similar to named restore points.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude can inspect status and diffs, propose commits, and use Git commands when permitted.
whenNotToUse: Do not let Claude discard unrelated uncommitted work
Do not force-push casually
modules.enableDisable: Git is separate from Claude Code. Initialize it with Git commands. Disable automatic mutation by requiring Claude to show status and diff before commit or push.
modules.bad: Commit and push all changes.
modules.good: Show status and the complete diff. Identify unrelated changes. Do not commit until I approve the file list.
modules.exercise: Make two small edits, commit them separately, and undo one without losing the other.
modules.interviewQuestion: Why are Git diffs and focused commits important in agent-assisted development?
modules.advanced: Power users combine branches, worktrees, draft PRs, signed commits, and automated checks.
modules.success: You can inspect, commit, and safely reverse Claude-generated changes.
modules.summary: Git is the durable safety record for all changes.

quiz.question: What should you inspect before committing?
quiz.explanation: The diff shows the exact changed lines.

modules.title: Testing and evidence-first debugging
modules.objective: Prove bugs and fixes with evidence.
modules.simple: First reproduce the problem. Then find the cause. Finally keep a test that would fail if the bug returns.
modules.problem: Guessing at a fix can hide the symptom without solving the cause.
modules.analogy: A doctor checks symptoms and tests hypotheses before choosing treatment.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude can run tests, inspect logs, compare passing and failing cases, and edit code after evidence narrows the cause.
whenNotToUse: Do not change production code before reproducing the problem when reproduction is possible
modules.enableDisable: Test commands must exist in the project. Allow exact test commands; deny unrelated commands or external side effects.
procedure: Ask Claude for two competing hypotheses.
modules.bad: This test is flaky. Increase the wait time.
modules.good: Run the test repeatedly, compare failing and passing logs, identify shared state, and test the leading hypotheses before editing production code.
modules.exercise: Take a small intentional bug, reproduce it, write a failing test, fix it, and prove the test passes.
modules.interviewQuestion: What is evidence-first debugging, and how can an AI agent support it?
modules.advanced: Advanced systems add trace correlation, deterministic replay, fuzzing, mutation testing, and automated regression evaluation.
modules.success: The fix explains the evidence and a regression test protects the behaviour.
modules.summary: Reproduction comes before correction.

quiz.question: What should come before a bug fix?
quiz.explanation: Reproduction gives you a way to prove the fix.

modules.title: Sessions, context, clear, compact, resume, and handoff
modules.objective: Keep Claude focused and recover cleanly when context becomes noisy.
modules.simple: A session is one working conversation. Context is the information currently available to Claude. Long or mixed sessions can become confused.
modules.problem: Unrelated history and stale decisions reduce accuracy.
modules.analogy: A crowded desk makes it harder to find the correct paper. A handoff note lets you clean the desk without losing important facts.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code supports session controls such as starting fresh, resuming, compacting, and using durable files for task state.
whenNotToUse: Do not clear before saving important decisions
Do not keep every unrelated task in one session
modules.enableDisable: Session commands are available in the interactive interface. You can stop using a session by exiting; remove reliance on history by starting fresh and loading a handoff.
procedure: Notice repeated misunderstandings or forgotten constraints.
Write goal, decisions, changed files, tests, failures, and next step.
Compact or start a fresh session.
Ask the new session to validate the handoff against the repository.
failureModes: Important state kept only in chat
commonMistakes: Using clear as a magic fix
Saving full transcripts instead of structured state
modules.bad: Keep correcting the same confused session indefinitely.
modules.good: Write a 200-word HANDOFF.md with evidence, start fresh, and verify the next action before editing.
modules.exercise: Complete a task across two sessions using only a handoff file to transfer state.
modules.interviewQuestion: How do context windows and durable state affect agent reliability?
modules.advanced: Agent systems separate context, workflow state, long-term memory, and authoritative sources into different stores.
modules.success: A fresh session can continue correctly without the old transcript.
modules.summary: Keep durable progress outside chat and use fresh context deliberately.

quiz.question: When is clearing context safest?
quiz.explanation: The handoff preserves the information needed to continue.

phases.title: Phase 3 · Claude Code Power User
phases.description: Master daily interface features, configuration, CLAUDE.md, permissions, worktrees, background tasks, and automation.

modules.title: Slash commands, models, status, voice, and terminal productivity
modules.objective: Use the interactive interface efficiently without hiding important state.
modules.simple: Power-user features reduce repeated effort, but they should make project state more visible, not more magical.
modules.problem: Repeated navigation, unclear branch state, and long typed prompts waste time and cause mistakes.
modules.analogy: A car dashboard does not drive for you; it shows the state you need to drive safely.
modules.howClaudeImplements: The interface exposes commands for help, session control, model selection, status, and other workflow operations.
whenNotToUse: Do not install every customization at once
Do not hide permission or branch information
modules.enableDisable: Configure optional interface features in Claude Code settings. Remove or disable custom status, aliases, or voice tools when they add confusion or risk.
usage: Adopt one customization at a time
procedure: Configure visible directory and branch state.
Measure whether the customization removes steps.
Remove it if it adds confusion.
modules.bad: Install every community patch and plugin.
modules.good: Track one week of friction, add one small improvement, and keep it only if it measurably helps.
modules.exercise: Remove two repeated steps from a daily Claude Code workflow without broadening permissions.
modules.interviewQuestion: Which interface signals should an AI coding environment expose to prevent operational mistakes?
modules.advanced: Teams standardize status, model policy, shell environment, and session conventions across developers.
modules.success: You can use core commands quickly and always know the current folder, branch, and session state.
modules.summary: Interface mastery is useful when it increases visibility and reduces friction.

quiz.question: Why expose branch and dirty state?
options: To prevent changes in the wrong context
quiz.explanation: Visible state helps prevent coordination errors.

modules.title: CLAUDE.md from first rule to team memory
modules.objective: Create concise project instructions that measurably improve Claude's behaviour.
modules.simple: CLAUDE.md is a project instruction file. Put stable, non-obvious rules there—not the current task or generic advice.
modules.problem: Teams repeatedly correct the same commands, generated-file rules, and architecture conventions.
modules.analogy: It is a short operating card attached to a machine, not a full textbook or diary.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code loads instruction files from supported scopes and applies them as project guidance.
whenNotToUse: Temporary progress
Secrets
Generic advice
Huge project documentation
modules.enableDisable: Create the supported CLAUDE.md file in the appropriate scope. Disable a rule by removing or narrowing it; disable the file by renaming or deleting it after review.
procedure: List repeated corrections from recent tasks.
Run a task that previously failed.
Remove the rule if it does not help.
failureModes: Rules loaded at the wrong scope
modules.bad: Always write clean and secure code. Here is every file in the project.
modules.good: Never edit src/generated. Run npm run generate. Use npm test -- --runInBand on Windows CI.
modules.exercise: Create a three-rule CLAUDE.md, test it on a real task, and delete one rule that does not change behaviour.
modules.interviewQuestion: What belongs in CLAUDE.md, and how would you prevent instruction bloat?
modules.advanced: Monorepos use layered instruction files and progressive disclosure, while deterministic style rules move to hooks or linters.
modules.success: The file is short, scoped, current, and changes behaviour measurably.
modules.summary: CLAUDE.md is stable executable team memory, not a dumping ground.

quiz.question: Where should current task progress live?
options: A task handoff or state file
quiz.explanation: Progress is temporary state, not stable project guidance.

modules.title: Branches, worktrees, and parallel Claude sessions
modules.objective: Run parallel work without file collisions or unclear ownership.
modules.simple: A Git worktree gives another branch its own folder. Separate Claude sessions can then work without editing the same files.
modules.problem: Parallel agents or sessions overwrite shared files and create merge conflicts.
modules.analogy: Two mechanics need separate workbenches if they are repairing different parts at the same time.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude sessions operate in separate directories while Git tracks branches and later integrates changes.
whenNotToUse: Do not parallelize shared architecture decisions or overlapping file edits
modules.enableDisable: Create a Git worktree and start Claude inside it. Stop parallel work by exiting sessions and removing the worktree after changes are integrated or discarded.
procedure: Split the work into independent parts.
Create one branch and worktree per writer.
commonMistakes: Sending multiple agents to the same module
modules.bad: Ask four sessions to refactor the same service.
modules.good: One session maps tests, one reviews security, and one isolated worktree implements the approved change.
modules.exercise: Use two worktrees: one for a documentation edit and one for a test change, then integrate both.
modules.interviewQuestion: What limits useful parallelism in multi-agent software development?
modules.advanced: Orchestrators allocate worktrees, enforce file ownership, validate handoff schemas, and run integration gates automatically.
modules.success: No two writers own the same files and integrated tests pass.
modules.summary: Parallelize independent work; serialize shared decisions and integration.

quiz.question: When are two tasks safe to parallelize?
options: When they edit the same file
When they are independent and have clear integration checks
quiz.explanation: Independence and explicit integration are required.

modules.title: Headless mode, scripts, background work, and CI
modules.objective: Automate only bounded and proven Claude Code workflows.
modules.simple: Interactive work has a person watching. Headless or scripted work runs without continuous conversation, so inputs, outputs, permissions, timeouts, and stopping rules must be explicit.
modules.problem: Unattended agents can repeat mistakes, hang, or create external side effects.
modules.analogy: A machine left running overnight needs guards, sensors, a timer, and an emergency stop.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code can be invoked non-interactively or integrated into scripts and CI with structured prompts and outputs.
whenNotToUse: Ambiguous new workflows
Production deployment without approval
Unlimited retries
modules.enableDisable: Enable through the documented non-interactive or script interface. Disable by removing the scheduled/script invocation, revoking credentials, or turning off the CI job.
procedure: Run the workflow manually several times.
modules.bad: Let Claude fix and deploy anything CI finds.
modules.good: CI sends a bounded diff to a read-only reviewer, validates JSON findings, and posts a report for human review.
modules.exercise: Build a read-only script that asks Claude to classify a small diff and returns validated JSON.
modules.interviewQuestion: What controls are required before running an AI coding agent unattended?
modules.advanced: Production automation adds queues, idempotency, durable state, trace IDs, policy engines, cost controls, and human escalation.
modules.success: The automation stops predictably, produces auditable output, and cannot perform unintended external actions.
modules.summary: Automate a proven loop, not an unclear ambition.

quiz.question: What should be automated first?
quiz.explanation: Known loops have understood inputs, checks, and failures.

phases.title: Phase 4 · Claude Code Extensions
phases.description: Learn commands, hooks, skills, subagents, MCP, settings, and how to choose the right mechanism.

modules.title: Commands, hooks, skills, subagents, and MCP: what each one means
modules.objective: Choose the smallest Claude Code extension mechanism for a need.
modules.simple: Commands are reusable entry points. Hooks run deterministic actions at events. Skills package methods. Subagents isolate a separate worker. MCP connects external tools or data.
modules.problem: Using the wrong extension creates extra context, permissions, and maintenance.
modules.analogy: A command is a named recipe, a hook is an automatic door sensor, a skill is a toolbox guide, a subagent is a specialist worker, and MCP is a bridge to another building.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Each mechanism has a different trigger, context boundary, and authority model inside the Claude Code ecosystem.
whenNotToUse: Do not combine all mechanisms for one simple task
Do not add MCP when a narrow CLI already works
modules.enableDisable: Enable each mechanism through its supported configuration or file location. Disable by removing the registration/configuration and restarting or reloading the relevant session where required.
procedure: Classify each as instruction, command, event, method, isolated work, or external bridge.
Document how it is enabled and disabled.
Test one success and one failure.
commonMistakes: Installing large bundles because they may help
Using prose where a deterministic hook is better
Giving external tools write access by default
modules.bad: Install every extension pack and place all instructions in CLAUDE.md.
modules.good: Use one read-only release-check skill, keep formatting in a hook, and require approval before deployment.
modules.exercise: Map ten tasks to the correct extension type and justify each choice.
modules.interviewQuestion: How do hooks, skills, subagents, commands, and MCP differ in trigger and responsibility?
modules.advanced: Architects treat extensions as governed capabilities with owners, versions, observability, permissions, and retirement paths.
modules.success: You can explain and choose each mechanism without overlap.
modules.summary: Choose extensions by responsibility, trigger, and permission boundary.

quiz.question: What best fits automatic formatting after every edit?
quiz.explanation: Formatting is deterministic event-driven work.

modules.title: Build, enable, disable, test, and debug hooks
modules.objective: Create safe deterministic automation around Claude Code events.
modules.simple: A hook runs a defined command when a specific event happens. It should be small, predictable, fast, and easy to disable.
modules.problem: Some rules must be enforced automatically rather than remembered by the model.
modules.analogy: A smoke alarm reacts automatically to smoke; it does not reason about whether smoke is fashionable.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code invokes configured hook commands at supported lifecycle events and observes their output or exit status.
whenNotToUse: Complex judgement
Slow network workflows
Irreversible deployment
modules.enableDisable: Enable by adding the hook configuration. Disable by removing, commenting, or turning off the hook entry and restarting/reloading if required.
procedure: Create a script that reports the event.
Trigger it in a practice project.
Disable the hook and confirm it no longer runs.
commonMistakes: Putting AI reasoning inside a deterministic hook
modules.bad: A hook decides whether the entire architecture is good.
modules.good: A hook rejects edits to generated files or runs a formatter with a clear error message.
modules.exercise: Create a practice hook that detects a forbidden filename, test success and failure, then disable it.
modules.interviewQuestion: When is a deterministic hook preferable to a model instruction?
modules.advanced: Enterprise hooks can call policy engines, emit trace events, enforce signing, and operate inside hardened runners.
modules.success: The hook behaves predictably, logs clearly, and can be disabled without damaging the project.
modules.summary: Hooks enforce deterministic events; keep them narrow and reversible.

quiz.question: What quality is most important for a hook?
quiz.explanation: Hooks should produce predictable results at known events.

modules.title: Create reusable skills and commands
modules.objective: Package a proven workflow so it can be invoked consistently.
modules.simple: A reusable command gives a workflow a name. A skill captures the method, inputs, checks, and expected output.
modules.problem: Repeatedly rewriting the same prompt causes inconsistent behaviour.
modules.analogy: Instead of explaining a recipe every time, write a recipe card and give it a name.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code loads supported command or skill definitions and uses them when invoked or selected.
whenNotToUse: One-time tasks
Unstable workflows
Broad authority without checks
modules.enableDisable: Enable by placing or registering the definition in the supported location. Disable by removing or renaming it and reloading the session if necessary.
procedure: Create the smallest command or skill.
commonMistakes: Creating a skill before the workflow is understood
modules.bad: Create one skill that reviews, fixes, commits, pushes, and deploys.
modules.good: Create a read-only review skill that returns file, line, severity, evidence, and suggested check.
modules.exercise: Package a repeated README review workflow into a reusable command or skill.
modules.interviewQuestion: What makes an agent skill maintainable and safe?
modules.advanced: Team skill registries add ownership, semantic versions, permissions, test fixtures, quality metrics, and deprecation policies.
modules.success: The same input produces a consistent, reviewable workflow and output.
modules.summary: Package only workflows that already work reliably by hand.

quiz.question: When should a workflow become a skill?
quiz.explanation: A proven workflow has known inputs, checks, and failures.

modules.title: Create and use subagents
modules.objective: Use a separate specialist context for bounded work.
modules.simple: A subagent is a separate worker with its own instructions and context. It returns a result to the main session.
modules.problem: One session can become overloaded when it must research, implement, review, and test everything with the same assumptions.
modules.analogy: A lead engineer asks a security specialist to inspect one area and return a report.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code can delegate to configured or supported subagent contexts with specific roles, prompts, tools, and output expectations.
whenNotToUse: Overlapping writes
Simple tasks
Shared decisions that require one owner
modules.enableDisable: Enable by defining or invoking a supported subagent. Disable by removing the definition, stopping delegation, or restricting its tools.
procedure: Specify allowed files and output schema.
Compare with the main session's view.
failureModes: Writer and reviewer sharing the same assumptions
commonMistakes: Creating many agents without a dependency plan
modules.bad: Launch five agents on the same feature and merge whatever looks best.
modules.good: Use one read-only security subagent with a file boundary and line-level evidence requirements.
modules.exercise: Create a reviewer subagent for a small diff and manually verify every reported issue.
modules.interviewQuestion: When does a subagent improve reliability rather than add coordination overhead?
modules.advanced: Production orchestrators route tasks by capability, allocate isolated environments, validate handoffs, and score specialist outputs.
modules.success: The subagent completes a narrow task, produces evidence, and does not conflict with the main worker.
modules.summary: Subagents isolate cognition; use them only for separable work.

quiz.question: What is a good first subagent task?
options: Read-only review of a small diff
Rewrite the same files as the main agent
quiz.explanation: Read-only review is bounded and easy to verify.

modules.title: Connect external tools with MCP
modules.objective: Connect Claude Code to external capabilities safely.
modules.simple: MCP is a standard way to expose tools or data to Claude. The safest MCP tool is narrow, structured, and minimally privileged.
modules.problem: Claude cannot access every external system by default, and generic shell access is too broad.
modules.analogy: MCP is a controlled service window. Claude can request specific items through the window instead of entering the entire building.
modules.howClaudeImplements: An MCP server advertises tool schemas and resources; Claude Code connects as a client and invokes allowed operations.
whenNotToUse: When a narrow existing CLI is sufficient
For unrestricted database or production access
For unclear tool schemas
modules.enableDisable: Enable by configuring the MCP server connection. Disable by removing or turning off the server configuration and revoking its credentials.
procedure: Disable the server and verify access is removed.
modules.bad: Expose unrestricted SQL execution to Claude.
modules.good: Expose read-only get_ci_failure(run_id) returning job, step, log excerpt, and source URL.
modules.exercise: Design an MCP server with one read-only tool, one validation error, and a documented disable procedure.
modules.interviewQuestion: How would you secure an MCP integration for enterprise use?
modules.advanced: Enterprise MCP gateways add identity, policy enforcement, audit logs, tenant isolation, data-loss prevention, and tool certification.
modules.success: Claude can use one external capability without gaining unrelated authority.
modules.summary: MCP should expose a narrow bridge, not an open door.

quiz.question: What is the best first MCP tool?
quiz.explanation: Narrow read-only tools are easier to secure and verify.

phases.title: Phase 5 · Agent Engineering
phases.description: Learn what an agent is, how to create one, persistent goals, loops, state, memory, stopping conditions, tools, and evaluation.

modules.title: What is an agent?
modules.objective: Understand the minimum components of an AI agent.
modules.simple: An agent is a system that receives a goal, observes information, chooses an action, uses tools, checks the result, and continues or stops according to rules.
modules.problem: Calling every chatbot an agent hides the need for tools, state, feedback, and stopping conditions.
modules.analogy: A delivery driver has a destination, sees the road, chooses turns, uses a vehicle, checks progress, and stops when the package is delivered or escalates when the road is blocked.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code already provides a basic agent loop through project context, tool calls, observations, permissions, and iterative actions.
whenToUse: Work that needs observation and correction
whenNotToUse: A single factual answer
Irreversible work without supervision
Goals with no measurable completion
modules.enableDisable: Claude Code's interactive agent behaviour starts when you open a session and give a task. Stop it by denying actions, interrupting, exiting, or defining completion and hard limits.
procedure: Ask Claude to plan one next action at a time.
commonMistakes: Letting the model decide irreversible actions
modules.bad: Keep working until you think it is done.
modules.good: Fix the failing parser test. Stop when the named test and full parser suite pass, or escalate after three failed approaches.
modules.exercise: Draw the agent loop for a small bug fix and label goal, observation, action, check, stop, and escalation.
modules.interviewQuestion: What minimum components distinguish an agent from a one-shot LLM call?
modules.advanced: Production agents separate planner, executor, evaluator, state store, policy layer, and human escalation.
modules.success: You can explain an agent without using the word agent in the definition.
modules.summary: An agent is a bounded observe-decide-act-check loop around a goal.

quiz.question: Which element is essential for an agent?
quiz.explanation: An agent must act toward a goal and evaluate progress.

modules.title: How to create an agent in Claude Code
modules.objective: Build a small bounded agent using Claude Code primitives.
modules.simple: You create an agent by combining a goal, instructions, allowed tools, durable state, checks, and stopping rules. Claude Code is the runtime; files and configuration define the behaviour.
modules.problem: A prompt alone does not make a dependable agent.
modules.analogy: Hiring a worker requires a job description, tools, a checklist, a progress board, and rules for when to ask the manager.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Use a project folder, CLAUDE.md or scoped instructions, skills or commands, optional subagents/MCP, state files, tests, and permission settings.
whenNotToUse: Unbounded business goal
Direct production control
Tasks without reliable checks
modules.enableDisable: Enable by opening the project and invoking the agent workflow or command. Disable by removing its command/skill/configuration, revoking tools, or stopping the session/automation.
procedure: Allow only file reads and test metadata.
commonMistakes: Starting with a coding agent that can push
modules.bad: Create an autonomous developer that builds anything I ask.
modules.good: Create a read-only diff-review agent that examines at most ten changed files and returns evidenced JSON findings.
modules.exercise: Build a local read-only review agent and run it against three small diffs.
modules.interviewQuestion: How would you construct a bounded agent using Claude Code primitives?
modules.advanced: The same pattern can be externalized into an orchestrator with APIs, queues, persistent state, policy, evals, and multiple model providers.
modules.success: The agent has an explicit goal, authority boundary, state, evaluator, stop rules, and disable path.
modules.summary: A dependable agent is a system of controls around Claude, not merely a clever prompt.

quiz.question: What should a first custom agent be allowed to do?
options: Read and report within a narrow scope
quiz.explanation: Read-only bounded work is the safest starting point.

modules.title: Persistent goals versus finite tasks
modules.objective: Know when a system should perform one task or continue managing a goal.
modules.simple: A task ends after one defined result. A persistent goal continues across new observations until success, failure, a limit, or human escalation.
modules.problem: Long-running goals can loop forever or take harmful actions when stop conditions are unclear.
modules.analogy: ‘Plant one tree’ is a task. ‘Keep the garden healthy’ is a continuing goal that requires regular checks and clear rules.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Finite tasks can run in one session or command. Persistent goals require repeated scheduling, durable state, observations, and explicit continue/stop/escalate decisions.
whenToUse: Finite task for one code review or change
Persistent goal for monitored maintenance with reliable signals
whenNotToUse: Do not convert a simple one-shot job into a permanent agent
Do not run persistent goals without budgets and ownership
modules.enableDisable: Enable persistence through an external scheduler or repeated workflow. Disable it by turning off the schedule, revoking tools, or marking the goal closed in durable state.
procedure: Take one example such as test health.
Define the state recorded after each observation.
Add attempt, time, and cost limits.
Add an owner and disable switch.
commonMistakes: Using slogans such as ‘own the goal’ without mechanics
modules.bad: Keep improving code quality forever.
modules.good: Each night, inspect new changes for critical security findings. Stop after one report, notify only on verified high severity, and disable via the CI schedule toggle.
modules.exercise: Convert three vague persistent goals into state machines with continue, stop, and escalation reasons.
modules.interviewQuestion: How do persistent goals change state and control requirements compared with finite tasks?
modules.advanced: Persistent agents use event streams, durable state machines, idempotency keys, leases, budgets, ownership, and policy-based termination.
modules.success: You can describe exactly how a persistent goal continues, stops, escalates, and is disabled.
modules.summary: Persistence is an operational design choice, not a motivational phrase.

quiz.question: What does a persistent goal require that a one-shot task may not?
quiz.explanation: Persistence needs state across observations and controlled termination.

modules.title: Context, state, memory, and source of truth
modules.objective: Store information in the correct layer.
modules.simple: Context is what the model sees now. State records workflow progress. Memory keeps selected facts across runs. The source of truth is the authoritative system.
modules.problem: Mixing these layers creates stale facts, bloated prompts, and incorrect resumptions.
modules.analogy: Your desk is context, a task board is state, a notebook is memory, and the official database is the source of truth.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code uses the current conversation and files as context; agents can use JSON or databases for state and curated files or services for memory.
whenNotToUse: Do not store temporary task status in global instructions
Do not treat model memory as authoritative
modules.enableDisable: Enable durable state or memory by adding explicit stores. Disable a memory source by removing it from retrieval/configuration and deleting or expiring records according to policy.
procedure: List ten data items from an agent workflow.
Move stable validated guidance into a memory file.
Keep business truth in the source system.
Start a fresh session from minimal state.
modules.bad: Keep every conversation so the agent remembers everything.
modules.good: Store task status in structured state, validated conventions in curated memory, and fetch current facts from the source system.
modules.exercise: Design state and memory for a bug-fixing agent and demonstrate recovery in a fresh session.
modules.interviewQuestion: How do context, state, memory, and source of truth differ in an agent architecture?
modules.advanced: Production systems add schemas, versioning, provenance, TTL, conflict resolution, access control, and memory quality evaluation.
modules.success: A fresh run resumes correctly without loading the old transcript.
modules.summary: Use the right storage layer for the right kind of information.

quiz.question: Where should ‘task 4 passed’ live?
quiz.explanation: Completion progress is workflow state.

modules.title: Stopping conditions, evaluators, observability, and recovery
modules.objective: Ensure an agent can prove success, fail safely, and explain what happened.
modules.simple: A stopping condition decides when work ends. An evaluator checks the result. Observability records the steps. Recovery decides what happens after failure.
modules.problem: An agent can claim success falsely, retry forever, or fail without enough evidence to diagnose it.
modules.analogy: An exam has a finish time, a marking scheme, an answer sheet, and a process for retaking or escalating errors.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Tests, schemas, independent checks, logs, tool traces, attempt counters, and human gates can control the loop around Claude Code.
whenNotToUse: Do not rely only on the model saying DONE
Do not allow unlimited retries
modules.enableDisable: Enable logging and checks in the workflow or surrounding harness. Disable the agent through a kill switch, schedule toggle, permission revocation, or terminal state.
procedure: Set attempt, time, and cost limits.
Record each tool action and result.
commonMistakes: No distinction between model, tool, and data failure
modules.bad: Continue until confident and say DONE.
modules.good: Stop on passing acceptance checks, fail after three attempts or budget, and escalate permission or requirement ambiguity.
modules.exercise: Create and test a stopping policy for a small review agent, including forced timeout and evaluator failure.
modules.interviewQuestion: How would you prove an agent succeeded and diagnose why it failed?
modules.advanced: Production eval platforms compare versioned datasets, trace quality, cost, latency, safety, and human override rates across models and workflows.
modules.success: Every run ends in verified success, explicit failure, or owned escalation.
modules.summary: An agent is trustworthy only when its loop is observable and bounded.

quiz.question: Why is a completion phrase insufficient?
options: The model can emit it without independent proof
quiz.explanation: Success must be checked against external evidence.

phases.title: Phase 6 · Multi-Agent Engineering
phases.description: Design coordinators, specialists, handoffs, parallel execution, conflict control, and human gates.

modules.title: Orchestration and multi-agent systems
modules.objective: Coordinate multiple agents without multiplying confusion.
modules.simple: Orchestration decides who does what, in what order, with which tools, and how outputs are checked and integrated.
modules.problem: Multiple agents create duplicated work, conflicting edits, inconsistent decisions, and expensive communication.
modules.analogy: A construction project needs one plan, specialist teams, handoff documents, inspections, and a final integrator.
modules.howClaudeImplements: A lead session or external orchestrator delegates bounded work to subagents or separate Claude Code environments and validates their outputs.
whenNotToUse: Simple tasks
Shared file editing
Unresolved architecture decisions
No integration test
modules.enableDisable: Enable by invoking multiple subagents/sessions or an orchestrator. Disable by stopping delegation, cancelling workers, revoking tools, and closing queued tasks.
commonMistakes: Using more agents to solve ambiguity
modules.bad: Launch five agents and merge the best answer.
modules.good: One coordinator owns architecture; separate read-only agents review security and tests; one isolated writer implements; the coordinator integrates and verifies.
modules.exercise: Build a three-agent workflow for a small feature with coordinator, implementer, and reviewer roles.
modules.interviewQuestion: What are the main coordination costs and failure modes in multi-agent systems?
modules.advanced: Enterprise orchestrators use durable workflows, queues, leases, capability routing, policy, shared blackboards, and compensating actions.
modules.success: Each agent has a unique responsibility and every handoff has an acceptance check.
modules.summary: Multi-agent design is dependency management, not agent multiplication.

quiz.question: Who should own a shared architecture decision?
quiz.explanation: Shared decisions need one owner to avoid divergence.

modules.title: Guardrails, permissions, and human-in-the-loop gates
modules.objective: Place control where consequences become meaningful.
modules.simple: Guardrails block forbidden behaviour, permissions limit reachable actions, and human gates reserve consequential decisions for people.
modules.problem: One safety mechanism cannot cover every model, tool, data, and business failure.
modules.analogy: A bank uses locked doors, access cards, transaction limits, cameras, and manager approval—not one giant warning sign.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code permission rules, hooks, isolated environments, tool schemas, external policy, and explicit approval steps can work together.
whenNotToUse: Do not ask humans to approve harmless reads one by one
Do not automate irreversible actions solely because they are frequent
modules.enableDisable: Enable controls in settings, hooks, tool gateways, and orchestration rules. Disable agent authority by revoking credentials, stopping schedules, removing tools, or activating a kill switch.
procedure: Classify actions by reversibility and external impact.
modules.bad: Ask for approval on every read or allow all production actions.
modules.good: Automate local tests, allow read-only issue lookup, and require approval for push, deploy, deletion, and sending messages.
modules.exercise: Create a permission and human-gate matrix for a multi-agent release workflow.
modules.interviewQuestion: How do guardrails, permissions, and human approval differ?
modules.advanced: High-assurance systems add policy-as-code, dual control, tamper-evident audit, sandboxing, anomaly detection, and emergency shutdown.
modules.success: A mistaken or malicious instruction cannot reach unrelated secrets, files, or production systems.
modules.summary: Control must be placed at the point of consequence.

quiz.question: Which action most clearly needs a human gate?
quiz.explanation: Deployment has external and potentially irreversible impact.

phases.title: Phase 7 · AI Engineering
phases.description: Build dependable harnesses, tools, memory systems, knowledge pipelines, evaluations, and production operations.

modules.title: Harness engineering: the system around the model
modules.objective: Design every component required for reliable agent behaviour.
modules.simple: The model is one component. A production agent also needs context management, tools, state, memory, policy, evaluation, tracing, retries, stopping, and recovery.
modules.problem: A good demo can fail in production because the surrounding system is missing.
modules.analogy: A powerful engine does not make a safe car without brakes, steering, sensors, fuel control, and a dashboard.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code can prototype the model-tool loop; production harnesses often externalize orchestration, state, policy, and observability into services.
whenNotToUse: Do not build a large harness for a simple one-shot task
modules.enableDisable: Enable components incrementally. The complete system must include a master kill switch, credential revocation, queue pause, and workflow cancellation.
failureModes: Model failure confused with tool failure
modules.bad: Use a smarter model and keep retrying.
modules.good: Design explicit state, typed tools, outcome evaluators, bounded retries, traces, and a human escalation path.
modules.exercise: Create a harness diagram and failure table for a release-review agent.
modules.interviewQuestion: What components belong in an agent harness beyond the model?
modules.advanced: Mature platforms provide reusable orchestration, tool gateways, memory services, policy, evaluation, and observability across many agents.
modules.success: Every system arrow has an owner, observable output, failure path, and shutdown control.
modules.summary: Reliability comes from the harness around the model.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a production harness from a demo?
options: Explicit state, safety, feedback, and observability
quiz.explanation: Production reliability depends on the surrounding system.

modules.title: Tool design for agents
modules.objective: Give agents narrow and predictable capabilities.
modules.simple: A good tool does one coherent job, accepts validated input, returns structured output, fails clearly, and cannot affect unrelated resources.
modules.problem: Broad tools make model mistakes dangerous and difficult to diagnose.
modules.analogy: A surgeon uses a specific instrument, not a box labeled ‘do anything.’
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code can call shell commands, built-in tools, skills, and MCP operations; the safest interfaces constrain each capability.
whenNotToUse: Do not expose generic shell or SQL when a narrow operation is possible
modules.enableDisable: Register tools through the supported mechanism. Disable by removing configuration, revoking credentials, or denying the tool in policy.
procedure: Split it into read and write tools.
modules.bad: execute(command: string)
modules.good: get_ci_failure(run_id) -> {job, step, excerpt, source_url} with read-only access and timeout.
modules.exercise: Redesign a generic database tool into three narrow operations with schemas and permission boundaries.
modules.interviewQuestion: What properties make a tool interface agent-friendly and safe?
modules.advanced: Enterprise tool gateways add policy evaluation, tenancy, rate limits, semantic schemas, replay protection, and end-to-end audit.
modules.success: Invalid calls fail clearly and the tool cannot reach unrelated data or actions.
modules.summary: Narrow tools make agent behaviour safer and more observable.

quiz.question: What is preferable to a generic shell tool?
quiz.explanation: Narrow operations reduce ambiguity and authority.

modules.title: Knowledge, retrieval, memory, and provenance
modules.objective: Provide relevant knowledge without creating unsupported truth.
modules.simple: Retrieval finds useful source material for the current task. Memory preserves selected information. Provenance shows where each claim came from.
modules.problem: Agents confidently repeat stale or unsupported information when sources and freshness are unclear.
modules.analogy: A researcher keeps citations so every conclusion can be checked against the original document.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code can search files and connected tools; production systems use indexes, knowledge graphs, databases, and memory stores.
whenNotToUse: Do not store everything
Do not treat generated summaries as primary evidence
modules.enableDisable: Enable knowledge sources in retrieval configuration. Disable by removing the source, revoking access, deleting indexed data, or applying expiry and retention rules.
modules.bad: Generate hundreds of linked notes and trust them.
modules.good: Build an isolated sourced knowledge set, attach provenance, sample-check claims, and keep deletion reversible.
modules.exercise: Create a five-document knowledge workflow with citations, conflict handling, refresh, and deletion steps.
modules.interviewQuestion: How would you design retrieval and memory so an agent can justify its answers?
modules.advanced: Advanced architectures combine hybrid retrieval, graphs, semantic layers, temporal validity, access controls, feedback, and memory quality scoring.
modules.success: Every important claim is traceable to an accessible source and can be refreshed or removed.
modules.summary: Knowledge is trustworthy only when it is sourced, current, and governed.

quiz.question: What prevents unsupported knowledge synthesis?
quiz.explanation: Provenance lets users verify claims against original evidence.

modules.title: Production evaluation, tracing, cost, latency, and operations
modules.objective: Measure and operate agent systems in production.
modules.simple: Evaluation measures outcome quality. Tracing explains the path. Operations keep the system available, affordable, secure, and recoverable.
modules.problem: A workflow that succeeds in a demo may regress with new models, prompts, tools, or data.
modules.analogy: An airline measures safe arrival, records the flight path, tracks fuel and delays, and investigates incidents.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code experiments can generate task traces and test evidence; production platforms capture structured events across components.
whenNotToUse: Do not judge production readiness from one successful prompt
modules.enableDisable: Enable telemetry and eval jobs with privacy controls. Disable or sample telemetry according to policy; never remove essential safety audit without an approved alternative.
procedure: Measure quality, cost, latency, and failures.
modules.bad: It worked five times, so deploy everywhere.
modules.good: Run a versioned task set, inspect traces, compare quality/cost/latency, canary the change, and keep rollback ready.
modules.exercise: Build a ten-case evaluation set for a review agent and compare two prompt versions.
modules.interviewQuestion: Which metrics and traces are required to operate an agent reliably?
modules.advanced: Mature programs use online/offline evals, red-team suites, causal incident analysis, SLOs, budget enforcement, and continuous calibration.
modules.success: A regression is detected, explained, and rolled back using evidence.
modules.summary: Production agents require continuous measurement, not one-time confidence.

quiz.question: What does tracing add beyond a pass/fail score?
options: The execution evidence explaining the result
quiz.explanation: Traces show where and why the outcome was produced.

phases.title: Phase 8 · AI Architecture
phases.description: Design secure, scalable, governed, and cost-aware enterprise agent platforms.

modules.title: Enterprise agent architecture
modules.objective: Design an enterprise platform that supports many governed agent workflows.
modules.simple: An enterprise agent platform separates users, models, orchestration, tools, data, policy, memory, evaluation, and operations into governed layers.
modules.problem: Independent agent projects duplicate integrations, leak data, create inconsistent controls, and become impossible to operate.
modules.analogy: A city needs roads, utilities, zoning, emergency services, and laws—not a separate infrastructure system for every building.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Claude Code remains a developer and local agent interface, while enterprise services provide identity, model routing, tool gateways, orchestration, state, memory, policy, evals, and audit.
whenNotToUse: Do not build a platform before validating real workflows
Do not centralize every experiment prematurely
modules.enableDisable: Enable capabilities through governed onboarding and policy. Disable at multiple levels: user, agent, tool, credential, tenant, model, workflow, queue, and platform kill switch.
procedure: Draw trust boundaries and data flows.
commonMistakes: Architecture driven by tools rather than use cases
modules.bad: Give every team a model key and let them connect anything.
modules.good: Provide governed model access, typed tool gateways, isolated state, policy enforcement, audit, evals, and layered kill switches.
modules.exercise: Design a reference architecture for three agent use cases with different risk levels and shared platform services.
modules.interviewQuestion: What layers and trust boundaries belong in an enterprise agent platform?
modules.advanced: Architects evaluate multi-region resilience, sovereign data, model portability, confidential computing, policy proofs, and organizational operating models.
modules.success: The architecture supports experimentation while preserving identity, data, policy, audit, reliability, and shutdown control.
modules.summary: Enterprise AI architecture turns isolated agents into governed platform capabilities.

quiz.question: What should an enterprise platform centralize first?
quiz.explanation: Identity, tool access, policy, audit, and evaluation benefit most from shared governance.

modules.title: Capstone: design and build a production-ready agent system
modules.objective: Apply the complete curriculum to one working system.
modules.simple: Build a bounded agent, connect safe tools, store state, evaluate results, trace execution, add human gates, and document how to operate and disable it.
modules.problem: Knowledge remains shallow until all pieces work together under success and failure conditions.
modules.analogy: A pilot proves skill by completing a supervised flight, not by memorizing instrument names.
modules.howClaudeImplements: Use Claude Code to design, implement, test, review, and document the system while keeping external control in the harness.
whenNotToUse: Do not choose a production-critical first capstone
Do not omit failure testing
modules.enableDisable: The capstone must include documented start, pause, resume, cancel, credential revoke, data deletion, and emergency shutdown procedures.
modules.bad: Build an agent that can do everything.
modules.good: Build a bounded incident-triage agent that reads approved logs, produces evidenced findings, stores workflow state, and requires approval before creating an external ticket.
modules.exercise: Deliver the complete capstone with repository, architecture diagram, threat model, eval report, operations runbook, and demonstration.
modules.interviewQuestion: Walk through the architecture, controls, evaluation, failure handling, and shutdown procedure of an agent system you built.
modules.advanced: Extend the capstone with multi-tenancy, model routing, online evaluation, policy-as-code, and disaster recovery.
modules.success: An independent reviewer can run, verify, fail, recover, and disable the system using your documentation.
modules.summary: The final proof is a system that works, fails safely, explains itself, and can be stopped.

quiz.question: What must a production capstone demonstrate?
options: Success, failure, recovery, governance, and shutdown
quiz.explanation: Production readiness requires evidence across normal and abnormal operation.
